mcq.q: Computer architecture refers to attributes visible to the programmer, such as:
mcq.a: The instruction set and addressing modes
x: Memory chip voltage is a physical electrical detail of the hardware implementation, not an attribute the programmer sees in the architecture.
Cooling methods are a physical thermal design concern of the hardware, not an architectural attribute visible to the programmer.
Cable routing is a physical wiring and assembly concern inside a machine, not something the programmer sees in the architecture.
mcq.e: The instruction set and addressing modes are the attributes visible to the programmer, defined by the architecture rather than by its physical implementation.

mcq.q: Which architecture uses one memory for both instructions and data?
x: The Harvard architecture uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data, not one memory shared by both.
A hybrid design with separate instruction and data caches, not the classic single-memory model the question asks about.
Not the answer here: Dataflow is an execution model driven by operand availability, not a stored-program design with one memory for instructions and data.
mcq.e: Von Neumann architecture stores instructions and data together in one memory accessed over one set of buses, which is what the question describes.

mcq.q: The limitation of using a single bus for instructions and data is known as the:
x: Not the answer here: Harvard gap is not a recognized term for this limitation; the Harvard design is the one with separate memories.
Not the answer here: the Moore wall refers to limits in transistor scaling, not to a bus shared by instructions and data.
Amdahl's Law describes speedup limited by the serial fraction of a program, not a memory bus bottleneck.
mcq.e: The Von Neumann bottleneck is the throughput limit caused by sharing one memory and bus between instructions and data, which is the limitation named here.

mcq.q: Which architecture has separate memories for instructions and data?
x: Von Neumann uses one memory and one bus shared by instructions and data, not separate memories for each.
Neural refers to neural network or neuromorphic designs, not a memory organization with separate instruction and data memories.
Not the answer here: Hybrid is not a specific memory architecture name; separate instruction and data memories define the Harvard design.
mcq.e: Harvard architecture uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so both can be accessed at the same time.

mcq.q: Which part of the CPU performs arithmetic and logic operations?
x: The control unit directs and sequences operations by issuing control signals, not performing the arithmetic and logic itself.
Cache is a small fast memory holding recently used data, not the unit that computes arithmetic and logic results.
A bus is a set of wires carrying data, addresses and control signals between components, not a unit that computes results.
mcq.e: The arithmetic logic unit performs arithmetic and logic operations on data, which is its defined role inside the CPU.

mcq.q: Which part of the CPU decodes instructions and issues control signals?
x: The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations on data, not decoding instructions or issuing control signals.
A register file is a set of small fast storage locations for operands and results, not the unit that decodes instructions.
The clock generates timing pulses that synchronize operations, not decoding instructions or issuing control signals.
mcq.e: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and issues control signals that direct the other CPU components.

mcq.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to execute?
x: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being executed, not the address of the next one.
The memory address register holds the address for a memory read or write, not the address of the next instruction.
The accumulator holds intermediate arithmetic results in some designs, not the address of the next instruction.
mcq.e: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, so it is the register the question describes.

mcq.q: Which register holds the instruction currently being executed?
x: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not the instruction currently being executed.
The memory data register holds data moving to or from memory, not the instruction being executed.
The stack pointer tracks the top of the call stack in memory, not the instruction currently being executed.
mcq.e: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed, which matches the question.

mcq.q: The correct order of the basic instruction cycle is:
x: An instruction must be fetched from memory before it can be decoded, so decode cannot come first.
An instruction must be decoded before its operation can be executed, so decode cannot come after execute.
Storing comes after execution, not first, and an instruction must be fetched before anything else happens.
mcq.e: The basic instruction cycle fetches an instruction, decodes it, executes it, and then stores the results.

mcq.q: A 32-bit address bus can address up to:
x: 2 GB corresponds to 31 address bits, not the full 32-bit address space.
8 GB needs 33 address bits, more than a 32-bit address bus can reach.
16 GB needs 34 address bits, which a 32-bit address bus cannot address.
mcq.e: A 32-bit address bus gives 2 to the power 32 bytes, which is 4 GB when each address names one byte.

mcq.q: x86 is an example of which type of ISA?
x: RISC uses simple fixed-length load/store instructions, which x86 does not follow, so it is not the answer.
VLIW issues several operations per long instruction scheduled by the compiler, which is not how x86 is designed.
A stack machine keeps operands on a stack rather than in general registers, which is not the x86 design.
mcq.e: x86 uses many complex instructions with variable lengths and memory operands, which is the CISC design.

mcq.q: Which ISA do Apple Silicon chips and most smartphones use?
x: x86 is the CISC instruction set used in most PCs and servers, not the one in Apple Silicon or most phones.
PowerPC is a RISC instruction set used in older Apple systems and some servers, not in Apple Silicon or most smartphones.
MIPS is a RISC instruction set used in some routers and embedded devices, not in Apple Silicon or most smartphones.
mcq.e: ARM is the RISC instruction set used in Apple Silicon chips and in most smartphone processors.

mcq.q: Intel's implementation of simultaneous multithreading is called:
x: Turbo Boost raises clock speed dynamically when thermal and power limits allow, not simultaneous multithreading.
SpeedStep is Intel's dynamic frequency and voltage scaling for power saving, not simultaneous multithreading.
vPro is Intel's business manageability and security platform, not a multithreading technology.
mcq.e: Hyper-Threading is Intel's implementation of simultaneous multithreading, which runs two threads on one physical core.

mcq.q: Which memory is the fastest in a computer?
x: L1 cache is very fast but slower than registers, sitting in the cache hierarchy below the register level.
RAM is much slower than registers and cache, so it is not the fastest memory in the computer.
SSD is persistent storage far slower than RAM and cache, not the fastest memory.
mcq.e: Registers are the fastest memory, located inside the CPU core and accessed in about one clock cycle.

mcq.q: In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block maps to:
x: That describes a fully associative cache, where a block can go in any line, not a direct-mapped cache.
A set of lines describes a set-associative cache, where a block maps to one set and can go in any line within that set.
A direct-mapped cache gives each block a fixed line, so it does not have no fixed line.
mcq.e: In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block can go into only one specific cache line, determined by its address.

mcq.q: SRAM is typically used for:
x: Main memory is usually DRAM, which is denser and cheaper per bit than SRAM, so SRAM is not the typical choice there.
Mass storage uses flash or magnetic media for large capacity, not fast SRAM that is costly per bit.
BIOS firmware is stored in non-volatile ROM or flash, not in SRAM cache.
mcq.e: SRAM is fast but costs more per bit, which makes it suitable for CPU caches.

mcq.q: DRAM requires:
x: DRAM is volatile and needs continuous power, so it does not require no power; the refresh need comes from leaking charge.
Ultraviolet erasure applies to EPROM chips, not DRAM, which is not erased by ultraviolet light.
DRAM is a solid-state chip with no moving parts, so mechanical parts are not required.
mcq.e: DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor that leaks over time, so it must be refreshed periodically.

mcq.q: Which company developed CUDA?
x: AMD developed ROCm and HIP as its GPU computing platform, not CUDA.
Intel developed oneAPI and its own GPU computing efforts, not CUDA.
Qualcomm designs mobile SoCs and Adreno GPUs and did not create CUDA.
mcq.e: CUDA is Nvidia's parallel computing platform and programming model for its GPUs.

mcq.q: Who is the CEO of Nvidia?
x: Lisa Su is the CEO of AMD, not Nvidia.
Pat Gelsinger was the CEO of Intel, not Nvidia.
Satya Nadella is the CEO of Microsoft, not Nvidia.
mcq.e: Jensen Huang is the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, which is the correct answer.

mcq.q: Who is the CEO of AMD?
x: Jensen Huang leads Nvidia, not AMD.
Lip-Bu Tan became Intel's CEO in March 2025, not AMD's.
Cristiano Amon is the CEO of Qualcomm, not AMD.
mcq.e: Lisa Su is the CEO of AMD, which is the company the question asks about.

mcq.q: Which company is the world's largest contract chipmaker?
x: Samsung Foundry is a major contract chipmaker but smaller than TSMC by revenue and market share.
Intel Foundry is Intel's contract manufacturing arm, which is much smaller than TSMC in foundry share.
GlobalFoundries is a significant foundry but is smaller than TSMC, so it is not the largest.
mcq.e: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, manufacturing chips designed by other companies.

mcq.q: Which company is the only maker of EUV lithography machines?
x: Applied Materials makes deposition and etch equipment, not EUV lithography machines.
Tokyo Electron makes coating, developing and etch equipment, not EUV lithography systems.
Canon makes lithography tools, but not EUV machines; its tools serve older process nodes.
mcq.e: ASML is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used for leading-edge chips.

mcq.q: Apple's in-house computer chips are branded as:
x: Ryzen is AMD's consumer CPU brand, not Apple's.
Snapdragon is Qualcomm's mobile chip brand, not Apple's.
Exynos is Samsung's mobile chip brand, not Apple's.
mcq.e: Apple's in-house chips for Macs and iPads are branded Apple Silicon, using the M-series name.

mcq.q: Qualcomm's mobile chip brand is:
x: Dimensity is MediaTek's mobile chip brand, not Qualcomm's.
Exynos is Samsung's mobile chip brand, not Qualcomm's.
Kirin is Huawei's mobile chip brand, not Qualcomm's.
mcq.e: Snapdragon is Qualcomm's mobile system-on-chip brand used in many Android phones.

mcq.q: Which quantum algorithm threatens RSA encryption?
x: Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup for unstructured search, which weakens symmetric keys more than it breaks RSA.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths on classical computers and is not a quantum attack on encryption.
Kruskal's algorithm builds minimum spanning trees on classical computers and has no role in breaking RSA.
mcq.e: Shor's algorithm can factor large integers efficiently on a quantum computer, which threatens the RSA encryption scheme.

mcq.q: A quantum bit is called a:
x: Qbyte is not a standard term for a quantum unit; the quantum bit is the qubit.
Quint is not a standard quantum term; the quantum bit is called a qubit.
Photon bit is not the standard name; photons can implement qubits, but the unit itself is the qubit.
mcq.e: A qubit is the quantum counterpart of a bit and can be in a superposition of 0 and 1.

mcq.q: FPGA stands for:
x: Not the answer here: this is not the standard expansion of FPGA, which is field-programmable gate array.
Fixed is wrong, since the defining feature of an FPGA is that its logic is field-programmable, not fixed.
Not the answer here: this is not the standard expansion; FPGA is a field-programmable gate array.
mcq.e: FPGA stands for Field-Programmable Gate Array, a chip whose logic can be reconfigured after manufacturing.

mcq.q: Which chip is custom-designed for one specific application?
x: An FPGA is reconfigurable and can be reprogrammed for many tasks, so it is not designed for one specific application.
A CPU is general-purpose and runs many programs, not a chip custom-designed for one application.
A GPU is a general-purpose parallel processor used for many workloads, not a single-application custom chip.
mcq.e: An ASIC is an application-specific integrated circuit designed for one task, which gives it high efficiency for that task.

mcq.q: A device that provides backup power during outages is a:
x: A PSU converts power inside the computer and does not supply backup power during an outage.
A KVM switch lets one keyboard, video and mouse control multiple computers, not provide backup power.
AVR, or automatic voltage regulation, corrects voltage fluctuations but does not provide battery backup on its own.
mcq.e: A UPS, or uninterruptible power supply, provides battery backup power during outages to keep equipment running.

mcq.q: The unit measuring floating-point operations per second is:
x: MIPS counts millions of instructions per second, which is not specific to floating-point operations.
CPI is cycles per instruction, a ratio rather than a rate of operations per second.
RPM is revolutions per minute, used for disk spindle speed, not for computing operations.
mcq.e: FLOPS, floating-point operations per second, measures computing performance for numerical workloads.

mcq.q: Which ISA family uses simple, fixed-length instructions and load/store architecture?
x: CISC uses complex, variable-length instructions that can access memory directly, not simple fixed-length load/store instructions.
VLIW packs several operations into one very long instruction scheduled by the compiler, not the simple RISC design described.
EPIC relies on compiler-scheduled parallelism, a design related to VLIW, rather than the simple fixed-length RISC design.
mcq.e: RISC uses simple fixed-length instructions and a load/store architecture, which is what the question describes.

mcq.q: Which of these is an open-standard RISC instruction set originated at UC Berkeley?
x: ARM is a proprietary RISC instruction set licensed by Arm Ltd, not an open standard originating at UC Berkeley.
MIPS is a RISC instruction set that originated at Stanford and is commercially licensed, not the Berkeley open standard.
x86-64 is a CISC extension of x86, not a RISC instruction set, and it is not an open standard from Berkeley.
mcq.e: RISC-V is an open-standard RISC instruction set that began at UC Berkeley, which is what the question asks for.

mcq.q: Which pipeline hazard occurs due to a branch instruction?
x: A data hazard happens when an instruction needs a result not yet produced by an earlier instruction, not because of a branch.
A structural hazard happens when two instructions need the same hardware resource at the same time, not because of a branch.
Not the answer here: memory hazard is not a standard pipeline hazard class; a branch causes a control hazard.
mcq.e: A control hazard happens when a branch changes the program flow, so the following instructions are not known in time.

mcq.q: Which pipeline hazard occurs when two instructions need the same hardware resource?
x: A data hazard comes from one instruction depending on the result of another, not from competition for hardware.
A control hazard comes from branches changing the flow of execution, not from competition for a hardware unit.
Not the answer here: branch hazard is not the standard term; the branch-related hazard is the control hazard.
mcq.e: A structural hazard occurs when two instructions compete for the same hardware resource in the same cycle.

mcq.q: Which principle explains why caches work by reusing recently accessed data?
x: Not the answer here: spatial parity is not a standard term; reuse of recently accessed data is called temporal locality.
Amdahl's Law concerns speedup from the serial fraction of a program, not reuse of recently accessed data.
The Pareto principle is the 80/20 observation about distribution of effects, not the locality principle behind caching.
mcq.e: Temporal locality means recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon, and caches exploit this reuse.

mcq.q: A cache that allows a block to be placed in any line is:
x: A direct-mapped cache gives each block exactly one possible line, not any line.
A one-way set-associative cache is equivalent to direct-mapped, where each block has only one possible line.
Write-through is a write policy that updates memory on each write, not a cache placement scheme.
mcq.e: A fully associative cache lets any memory block be placed in any cache line, which gives the most placement flexibility.

mcq.q: Which write policy updates both cache and main memory on every write?
x: Write-back updates only the cache and defers the memory write until eviction, so it does not update memory on every write.
Write-around sends writes straight to memory without placing them in the cache, so it does not update both on every write.
Write-allocate is a policy for loading a block into the cache on a write miss, not a rule that updates memory on every write.
mcq.e: Write-through writes every update to both the cache and main memory immediately, which keeps memory consistent.

mcq.q: Which flash type is used in SSDs and USB drives?
x: NOR flash supports random access for code execution and is used in firmware, not typically for bulk storage in SSDs and USB drives.
PROM is one-time programmable read-only memory, not reusable flash storage.
Mask ROM is fixed at manufacture, so it cannot store changing data as SSDs and USB drives must.
mcq.e: NAND flash is the high-density non-volatile memory used in SSDs and USB drives.

mcq.q: Flynn's taxonomy classification of a typical GPU's vector processing is:
x: SISD is a single instruction operating on a single data stream, as in a classic scalar processor, not many data elements at once.
MISD applies multiple instruction streams to one data stream, a rare class that does not describe GPU vector processing.
MIMD runs multiple independent instruction streams on multiple data streams, as in multicore CPUs, not one instruction across vector lanes.
mcq.e: SIMD applies one instruction to many data elements at the same time, which matches the vector-style parallel processing of a GPU.

mcq.q: Flynn's classification of a multicore processor running different programs on different data is:
x: SISD has one instruction stream and one data stream, as in a single-core scalar processor, not several programs running at once.
SIMD applies one instruction to many data items in lockstep, not separate programs running independently on each core.
MISD applies multiple instruction streams to a single data stream, which does not describe independent programs working on different data.
mcq.e: MIMD means multiple instruction streams operate on multiple data streams independently, which fits cores running different programs on different data.

mcq.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location to be read or written?
x: The memory data register holds the data read from or written to memory, not the address of that location.
The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not the address used for a data read or write.
The instruction register holds the current instruction, not a memory address for a read or write.
mcq.e: The memory address register holds the address used for a memory read or write, which is its role in this question.

mcq.q: Which register holds data being transferred to or from memory?
x: The memory address register holds the address of the location, not the data being transferred.
The instruction register holds the current instruction being executed, not data moving to or from memory.
The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not data transferred to or from memory.
mcq.e: The memory data register holds the data being moved to or from memory during a read or write operation.

mcq.q: Which bus carries read/write and clock signals?
x: The address bus carries the memory or device address being accessed, not read/write or clock signals.
The data bus carries the data being transferred, not the control signals that coordinate the transfer.
An expansion bus connects add-on cards or peripheral slots, not the internal read/write and clock signals.
mcq.e: The control bus carries read and write signals and clock timing between the CPU, memory and other components.

mcq.q: Which company created the x86-64 (AMD64) extension?
x: Intel designed the original x86 and later adopted AMD64, so it did not create the 64-bit extension described here.
ARM designs and licenses the ARM architecture and did not create the x86-64 extension.
IBM is known for POWER and mainframe architectures, not for the x86-64 extension.
mcq.e: AMD created the AMD64 extension, now known as x86-64, which Intel later adopted.

mcq.q: Which endianness stores the least significant byte at the lowest address?
x: Big-endian stores the most significant byte at the lowest address, which is the opposite of the question.
Middle-endian is a mixed byte order used in a few historical systems, not the least-significant-byte-first layout named here.
Network order is big-endian by convention, so it stores the most significant byte first, not the least significant byte.
mcq.e: Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest memory address, as the question states.

mcq.q: CPU time is calculated as:
mcq.a: Instruction count x CPI x clock cycle time
x: Dividing instruction count by CPI gives neither cycles nor a valid time; it does not match the correct calculation.
Dividing CPI by clock rate ignores the instruction count, so it does not match the correct calculation.
Multiplying clock rate by instruction count ignores CPI and gives no valid time; it does not match the correct calculation.
mcq.e: CPU time equals instruction count times CPI times clock cycle time, which is the standard performance equation.

mcq.q: Amdahl's Law describes:
mcq.a: Speedup limited by the serial fraction
x: Transistor doubling describes Moore's Law, which concerns chip density growth, not speedup from enhancing part of a program.
Cache hit rate measures how often data is found in cache, not the overall speedup limit given by Amdahl's Law.
Bus width scaling concerns data transfer width in hardware, not the speedup limit from the serial part of a program.
mcq.e: Amdahl's Law gives the overall speedup from enhancing part of a program, and the unenhanced serial fraction limits that speedup.

mcq.q: Pipelining improves:
x: Pipelining does not shorten how long one instruction takes; it overlaps stages, so single-instruction latency is not what improves.
Memory capacity is the amount of storage, which pipelining does not change.
The clock cycle is not what pipelining is meant to improve; it overlaps instruction stages, which raises throughput.
mcq.e: Pipelining increases the number of instructions completed per unit time, which is throughput, while single-instruction latency is not reduced.

mcq.q: The classic 5-stage RISC pipeline stages are:
x: This puts write-back before memory access, which is not the standard stage order.
Not the answer here: these are not the standard names of the classic five stages.
Not the answer here: these are not the standard stage names of the classic five-stage RISC pipeline.
mcq.e: The classic five-stage RISC pipeline is instruction fetch, instruction decode, execute, memory access and write-back.

mcq.q: Accessing nearby memory addresses soon after one another is:
x: Temporal locality is reuse of recently accessed data at the same address, not access to nearby addresses.
Cache coherence keeps copies of shared data consistent across caches, not the pattern of nearby accesses.
Hit ratio is the fraction of accesses found in the cache, a performance measure rather than an access pattern.
mcq.e: Spatial locality means nearby addresses are likely to be accessed soon after one another, which is why caches load whole blocks.

mcq.q: Which interface carries NVMe SSDs?
x: SATA is the older storage interface used by many drives, which is slower and uses AHCI rather than NVMe over PCIe.
USB 2.0 is a peripheral interface far too slow for NVMe drives, so it is not the one that carries them.
PS/2 is a legacy keyboard and mouse connector, not a storage interface.
mcq.e: NVMe SSDs are carried over PCIe, which gives them far more bandwidth than SATA.

mcq.q: Which Nvidia GPU architecture came after Hopper?
x: Ampere came before Hopper, as the architecture of the A100 generation, not after it.
Volta came well before Hopper, so it is not the successor to Hopper.
Turing came before Ampere and Hopper, so it is not the architecture that followed Hopper.
mcq.e: Blackwell is Nvidia's GPU architecture that followed Hopper.

mcq.q: AMD's server CPU line is:
x: Ryzen is AMD's consumer and desktop CPU line, not its server line.
Xeon is Intel's server processor line, not AMD's.
Threadripper is AMD's high-end desktop and workstation line, not its server line, so it does not fit alone.
mcq.e: EPYC is AMD's server processor line, aimed at data centers.

mcq.q: Intel's server CPU line is:
x: Core Ultra is Intel's consumer and laptop processor line, not its server line.
EPYC is AMD's server line, not Intel's.
Atom is Intel's low-power line for tablets, embedded and small devices, not its server line.
mcq.e: Xeon is Intel's server and workstation CPU line.

mcq.q: The firmware that replaced the legacy BIOS with Secure Boot and GPT support is:
x: CMOS is a chip technology, and the name also refers to the small memory that stores BIOS settings, not the firmware that replaced BIOS.
POST is the Power-On Self-Test run during startup, not the firmware that replaced BIOS.
MBR is the older master boot record partition scheme, which GPT replaces, not the firmware itself.
mcq.e: UEFI is the firmware that replaced legacy BIOS and supports Secure Boot and GPT partitions.

mcq.q: Which memory technology holds data using a capacitor and transistor per bit?
x: SRAM stores each bit in a set of transistors without a capacitor that needs refreshing, not a capacitor and transistor per bit.
ROM is read-only memory that keeps its contents without power, not per-bit capacitor storage.
Flash stores charge in floating-gate transistors, not a capacitor and transistor per bit that needs refreshing.
mcq.e: DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor with a transistor, and it must be refreshed periodically.

mcq.q: Which ROM type is erased by exposing the chip to ultraviolet light?
mcq.e: EPROM uses a UV-transparent window for erasure. EEPROM is erased electrically, PROM is one-time programmable, and mask ROM is fixed at manufacture.
x: EEPROM is erased electrically, byte by byte, not by exposing the chip to ultraviolet light. The question describes UV erasure, which is EPROM.
PROM is programmable only once by the user and cannot be erased at all. UV exposure has no erasing effect on it.
Mask ROM is fixed at manufacture by the mask process and cannot be erased by any method. UV light does not apply to it.

mcq.q: Which Flynn class is rare and associated mainly with fault-tolerant systems?
mcq.e: MISD applies multiple instruction streams to the same data and is mostly seen in redundant fault-tolerant designs. Multicore and clusters are MIMD; GPUs and vector units are SIMD.
x: SISD is a single instruction stream on a single data stream, the ordinary uniprocessor model. It is not the rare fault-tolerant class in the question.
SIMD applies one instruction to many data items, as in GPUs and vector units. It is common, not the rare class the question describes.
MIMD runs multiple instruction streams on multiple data streams, as in multicore and cluster systems. It is the common parallel class, not MISD.

mcq.q: Which hardware component converts AC power from the wall outlet into DC power for computer parts?
mcq.e: The PSU converts AC mains power into the DC voltages that components use.
x: The motherboard connects components but does not convert mains power.
The chipset manages data flow between components.
A heat sink dissipates heat.

mcq.q: A superscalar processor is one that can:
mcq.a: Issue and execute more than one instruction per clock cycle
w: Run only one instruction at a time
Store instructions and data in separate memories
Use only registers and no main memory
mcq.e: Superscalar CPUs have multiple execution units so several instructions complete per cycle.
x: That describes a scalar, non-pipelined design.
That describes the Harvard architecture.
Every CPU also uses main memory.
